title: MLPC Retake 2024 - Complete Exam
subject: Machine Learning and Pattern Classification
description: All 43 questions from the six consecutive MLPC retake PDF exports created on July 9, 2024. Correct answers and short explanations are included. The original density-estimation and classifier dataset figures are broken in the source PDFs and are therefore noted but not embedded.

questions.question:
Consider Bayes' rule for classification:
\[
P(\omega_i \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x} \mid \omega_i)P(\omega_i)}{p(\mathbf{x})}.
\]
Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) containing 5000 fish.

Question 1
For any fish \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{D}\), \(p(\mathbf{x}) \leq 1/5000\).
questions.explanation: For continuous features, \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is a density and is not bounded by the empirical frequency \(1/5000\).

questions.question:
Consider Bayes' rule for classification:
\[
P(\omega_i \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x} \mid \omega_i)P(\omega_i)}{p(\mathbf{x})}.
\]
Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) containing 5000 fish.

Question 2
For any fish \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{D}\), \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is a vector with 100 values.
questions.explanation: \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is a scalar marginal density evaluated at the 100-dimensional vector x.

questions.question:

\]
Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) containing 5000 fish.

Question 3
For any \(\mathbf{x}\), \(\sum_i p(\mathbf{x} \mid \omega_i) = 1\).
questions.explanation: Class-conditional densities do not generally sum to one across classes for a fixed x.

questions.question:
Consider Bayes' rule for classification:
\[
P(\omega_i \mid \mathbf{x}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x} \mid \omega_i)P(\omega_i)}{p(\mathbf{x})}.
\]
Assume a classification problem with 5 fish classes, a 100-dimensional real-valued feature space, and a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) containing 5000 fish.

Question 4
\(P(\omega_1 \mid \mathbf{x})\) is a vector with 5 entries.
questions.explanation: \(P(\omega_1 \mid \mathbf{x})\) is one scalar posterior probability.

questions.question:
Consider the \(5 \times 5\) zero-one loss matrix \(\lambda\) for the classification problem above, learned prior and class-conditional distributions, and a Bayesian minimum-risk classifier.

Question 5
On any specific test set \(\mathcal{T}\), the minimum-risk classifier has exactly the same position in ROC space as a MAP classifier.
questions.explanation: With zero-one loss, minimizing conditional risk is equivalent to choosing the maximum posterior class (MAP).

questions.question:
Consider the \(5 \times 5\) zero-one loss matrix \(\lambda\) for the classification problem above, learned prior and class-conditional distributions, and a Bayesian minimum-risk classifier.

Question 6
\(\sum_i \sum_j \lambda_{ij} = 1\).
questions.explanation: A loss matrix is not required to have entries summing to one.

questions.question:
Consider the \(5 \times 5\) zero-one loss matrix \(\lambda\) for the classification problem above, learned prior and class-conditional distributions, and a Bayesian minimum-risk classifier.

Question 7
Multiplying every value in \(\lambda\) by 5 makes it an invalid loss function.
questions.explanation: Positive scaling preserves all risk comparisons and therefore the classifier's decisions.

questions.question:
Consider a \(k\)-nearest-neighbour classifier in a \(d\)-dimensional numeric feature space, with a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) containing \(N > 0\) instances of two classes and Euclidean distance.

Set \(k = N = |\mathcal{D}|\).

Question 14
The classifier will maximally overfit the training data.
questions.explanation: Using all N neighbours heavily smooths the classifier rather than maximally overfitting.

questions.question:

Set \(k = N = |\mathcal{D}|\).

Question 15
The resulting classifier has an expected accuracy of \(1/N\).
questions.explanation: The prediction is driven by the overall class majority, so accuracy is not generally \(1/N\).

Question 16
Every training example is classified into its correct class.
questions.explanation: Minority-class training examples are generally assigned to the global majority class.

Question 17
The resubstitution estimate on \(\mathcal{D}\) is \(1\).
questions.explanation: The resubstitution accuracy equals the proportion of the majority class, not necessarily 1.0.

Question 18
All test examples are classified into the same class.
questions.explanation: With \(k=N\), every query uses the full training set and receives the global majority class.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) and a set of discrete features \(\mathcal{F}\). It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 19
Combining several such trees into a random forest makes no sense because the trees rely on incompatible features.
questions.explanation: Random forests intentionally combine diverse trees built from different feature choices.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) and a set of discrete features \(\mathcal{F}\). It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 20
The randomly chosen feature split might have information gain zero.
questions.explanation: A randomly selected feature may be independent of the class labels and yield zero information gain.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) and a set of discrete features \(\mathcal{F}\). It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 21
Every such decision tree has training accuracy on \(\mathcal{D}\) higher than the default accuracy.
questions.explanation: A split may fail to improve on predicting the global majority class.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) and a set of discrete features \(\mathcal{F}\). It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 22
Every such decision tree has exactly the default accuracy on \(\mathcal{D}\).
questions.explanation: Some splits improve accuracy while others do not, so exact equality is not guaranteed.

questions.question:
A decision-tree learner receives a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) and a set of discrete features \(\mathcal{F}\). It randomly selects one feature, builds a one-level tree by splitting on that feature, and labels each resulting leaf with the majority class in that node.

Question 23
The resulting structure is not a decision tree.
questions.explanation: A one-level split with labelled leaves is a valid decision tree.

questions.question:
For the same two-class dataset, consider a feedforward neural network with inputs \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), one hidden unit with \(\tanh\) activation, and one output unit with identity activation. Classes are encoded as 0 (white) and 1 (black), training uses squared error, and the prediction is black when the output is greater than a threshold \(\tau\), and white otherwise. The weights are unrestricted.

Question 30
Increasing the threshold \(\tau\) cannot increase recall for class 0 on the training set.
questions.explanation: Raising \(\tau\) predicts white more often, which can increase recall for class 0.

questions.question:

Classes are encoded as 0 (white) and 1 (black), training uses squared error, and the prediction is black when the output is greater than a threshold \(\tau\), and white otherwise. The weights are unrestricted.

Question 31
The single hidden unit is unnecessary; a network without a hidden unit can learn the same function.
questions.explanation: The tanh hidden unit introduces a nonlinearity that a network without a hidden layer cannot generally reproduce.

Question 32
Setting \(\tau\) to 0 or 1 makes every possible input receive the same class from any model trained this way.
questions.explanation: The identity output is unbounded, so outputs may lie below 0 or above 1.

Question 33

questions.explanation: An identity-activation output trained with squared error is a real-valued score, not necessarily a calibrated probability.

Question 34
Different values of \(\tau\) for a fixed learned model can produce classifiers at different positions in ROC space.
questions.explanation: Changing the threshold changes the true-positive and false-positive rates.

questions.question:

Question 35
The output unit's prediction is always in \([0,1]\).
questions.explanation: Identity activation imposes no \([0,1]\) bound.

questions.question:
Model whether a football game is occurring as a hidden Markov model with
\[
\mathcal{S} = \{\mathrm{game}, \mathrm{no\ game}\}
\]
and observations
\[
\mathcal{O} = \{\mathrm{none}, \mathrm{cheer}, \mathrm{shout}, \mathrm{curse}, \mathrm{snore}\}.
\]
Use the matrix conventions from the lecture slides.

Question 36
What are the dimensions of the transition matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) (rows \(\times\) columns)?
questions.explanation: There are two hidden states, so the state-transition matrix is \(2 \times 2\).

Question 43
From which model component can the expected duration of a game, meaning consecutive time points with \(q_t = \mathrm{game}\), be estimated?

options.text: It cannot be estimated from the model

questions.explanation: Expected state duration is determined by the self-transition probability in A.
